posts.title: How to learn hiragana in two weeks
posts.excerpt: Forty-six letters in fourteen days sounds like a lot. Ten minutes a day, a pack of round stickers and one silly picture per letter make it easy.
posts.content:
Forty-six letters in fourteen days sounds like a lot. It is not, if you do a little every day and give every letter a story. This is the plan our Seed students follow in the Kana in Two Weeks course.

Ten minutes, every day

Long weekend sessions feel heroic and are forgotten by Wednesday. Ten minutes after breakfast, every day, is what works. Set a timer and stop when it rings.

One row at a time

  • Days 1 to 3: the vowels and the k-row
  • Days 4 to 7: the s, t and n rows
  • Days 8 to 11: the h, m and y rows
  • Days 12 to 14: the r and w rows, and the final n

Every time you finish a row, put a round sticker on your chart. It looks childish. It works.

By day nine I was reading the station names out loud on the train. Quietly, mostly.

Priya, Seed level

Draw a silly picture

Every letter gets a small drawing that makes its sound. The sillier, the better: your brain keeps what made you smile.

posts.title: Our hanami picnic, and the words we learned on the tarp
posts.excerpt: Forty students, three blue tarps and one very determined crow. Notes from the first week of spring term under the trees by the canal.
posts.content:
Every spring term begins the same way: no grammar on the first Friday, only a picnic under the cherry trees by the canal. Forty students, three blue tarps, a lot of rice balls and one very determined crow.

Words for the tarp

  • hanami: looking at the blossoms (and the picnic underneath them)
  • basho-tori: arriving early to save a good spot
  • kanpai: cheers
  • sakura fubuki: a snowstorm of falling petals

The Bloom class ran a quiz, the Seed class won it, and nobody is quite sure how.

I learned more Japanese in two hours on that tarp than in a month of apps.

Lucas, Bud level

posts.title: Listening practice with the radio on
posts.excerpt: You do not need to understand everything. Our teachers explain how to use background Japanese to train your ear without getting tired.
posts.content:
Real Japanese is fast. The good news: your ear learns speed long before your mouth does, and it learns it in the background.

Three rules

  • Play something you like, not something you should like
  • Listen for words you know, not for words you do not
  • Stop after twenty minutes, before it becomes noise

Try it while cooking. When a word you learned this week flies past, say it out loud. That small jump of recognition is the whole exercise.

posts.title: My first week, from the other side of the whiteboard
posts.excerpt: Kenta Ishida spent ten years in an office before he started teaching. Here is what surprised him in his first week in Room Ume.
posts.content:
I spent ten years writing very polite emails in an office in Shinjuku. Now I teach people how to write them. My first week in Room Ume surprised me three times.

Everyone is brave

Saying a new word out loud in front of strangers takes courage. My students do it forty times an hour.

Mistakes are the lesson

The best moment of the week was a wrong word: a student asked for “a cold umbrella” instead of “a cold drink”. We learned two words that day, and nobody will forget either.

Teach the Japanese you wish someone had taught you.

Haruka Mori, head teacher, on my first day

posts.title: Kanji radicals are like building blocks
posts.excerpt: Two thousand characters, but only about two hundred pieces. Learn the pieces first and new kanji start to look familiar.
posts.content:
Kanji look endless. They are not: most are built from a small set of parts called radicals, and around two hundred of them do most of the work.

Learn the pieces, then the words

A character with the water radical is often about water, a character with the tree radical is often about wood. Once you know the pieces, a new kanji stops being a picture and becomes a little puzzle.

  • Water: rivers, seas, washing, swimming
  • Tree: forests, desks, bridges
  • Person: rest, body, lend

posts.title: From zero to Bud level in a year
posts.excerpt: Amara arrived in Tokyo with three words of Japanese. A year later she gave a short speech at the autumn speech afternoon. She tells us how.
posts.content:
When I arrived in Tokyo I knew three words: hello, thank you and sorry. I used the last one a lot.

What helped

  • Two evening classes a week, even when I was tired
  • Friday tea, where I could practise without a textbook
  • Online Evenings when I travelled for work

A year later I gave a three-minute speech about my neighbourhood cat at the autumn speech afternoon. My teacher cried a little. So did I.

Nobody here laughs at you. They laugh with you, and then they teach you the right word.

Amara, Bud level

posts.title: Five polite phrases for your first week at work
posts.excerpt: The phrases you will hear (and need) before lunch on your first day in a Japanese office, explained by our Japanese for Work class.
posts.content:
Your first week in a Japanese office comes with its own small set of phrases. You will hear them before lunch on day one. Here are five, with what they really mean.

  • Yoroshiku onegaishimasu: nice to meet you, and thank you in advance for everything
  • Otsukaresama desu: thanks for your hard work (also: hello, goodbye, well done)
  • Shitsurei shimasu: excuse me, as you enter or leave
  • Kakunin shimasu: I will check
  • Osaki ni shitsurei shimasu: sorry for leaving before you

Practise them in the Japanese for Work class, where Daichi plays the strict manager with great enthusiasm.
